title: Adaptive commit curve mitigation playbook
content: Purpose:\nThis note captures a practical playbook for smoothing the financial and operational impact of uneven committed GPU capacity growth — specifically targeting the mid-term (3–12 month) window where customer commit curves are noisy and the risk of long periods of low utilization creates unit-cost volatility. It pairs a compact simulation approach with a set of concrete price and operational levers we can test quickly.
content_addendum:
Background and problem statement:
- Observed behavior: a cohort of mid-market customers commit in multi-month lumps (pilot -> scale -> plateau) rather than a steady ramp. That leads to extended low-utilization tails in dedicated pools when new commit waves miss timing.
- Consequence: reserved GPU amortization per effective workload token spikes for 6–10 weeks after a commit wave, increasing marginal unit costs and pushing internal margin below target.
- Goal: reduce realized unit-cost volatility for a given reserved pool while preserving attractive economics for customers who reserve capacity. Improve predictability for capacity planning and sales risk modeling.

Modeling assumptions (compact):
- Pool size represented in reserved-GPU-equivalents (rGEs). One rGE ~ one T4-equivalent workload baseline for our accounting.
- Baseline utilization measured as active-rGE-hours / reserved-rGE-hours. Historical baseline for test pool: 0.58 avg, 75th percentile 0.82, 25th percentile 0.32.
- Demand arrival per customer cohort approximated via piecewise-linear commit curve: ramp months 1–3, scale months 4–8, plateau months 9+. Add stochastic noise: month-to-month demand multiplicative factor ~ LogNormal(mu=0, sigma=0.18).
- Cost stack: amortized hardware + infra overhead + power + network + SW license = $X per rGE-hour (use linked sheet for exact values). Spot/ephemeral capacity available at discount D (30–50% lower cost) and can be used for burst/offpeak if tenancy allows.

Simulation approach (sheet: adaptiveCurveSim v1):
- Input: commit schedule (customer-level), pool reservation horizon, spot availability schedule, burst credit budget, typical seq-length and token-rate distribution.
- Runs: deterministic baseline + 1,000 Monte Carlo draws for stochastic noise.
- Outputs: per-month realized utilization, amortized $/effective-rGE-hour, per-token effective cost for 50th/90th percentile demand, tail risk (months where utilization < 40%).

Key mitigation levers to test (prioritized):
1) Commit curve smoothing credits (sales-facing): allow customers to phase-in committed capacity over 3 billing cycles with an amortization surcharge/discount curve. Tradeoff: slightly higher sticker for smoothing vs. higher volatility.
2) Internal buffer tranche (operational): set aside a small, pooled buffer (3–8% of total rGEs) with shorter amortization to absorb low-tail months.
3) Off-peak recapture pricing: shift low-utilization minutes to off-peak discounted buckets that count partially toward commit utilization (e.g., 40% credit for deep off-peak hours).
4) Dynamic overcommit insurance: allow short-term overcommit of reserved pools by blending reserved and spot capacity under a fallback SLA with explicit per-token surcharge when spot used.
5) Canary-decommit window: introduce a 30–60 day notification window for large decommits from enterprise customers, with optional phased decommit credits to smooth the pool.

Representative scenario outputs (summary numbers from initial sim run — illustrative):
- Scenario A (no mitigation): avg utilization 0.58, months with util<40% = 5 in 12, realized amortized cost per 1M tokens = $2,050 (90th pct $3,300).
- Scenario B (3% buffer + off-peak recapture): avg util 0.64, months<40% = 2, amortized cost per 1M tokens = $1,700 (90th pct $2,200).
- Scenario C (smoothing credits + dynamic overcommit): avg util 0.72, months<40% = 0–1, amortized cost per 1M tokens = $1,430 (90th pct $1,820).

Interpretation and commercial impact:
- Small operational buffers and explicit off-peak crediting deliver outsized stability gains relative to their capacity cost.
- Sales-facing smoothing credits may reduce churn risk by offering predictable near-term economics for customers onboarding; pricing needs to be set to keep present value of committed revenue similar while shifting some margin to the smoothing product.
- Dynamic overcommit reduces tail risk but requires careful SLA/contract language and usage accounting — treat as an advanced feature for mid-enterprise customers.

Implementation experiments (next 90 days):
1) Create a pilot product: "phased commit" offering for new customers with 3-month phase-in. Launch with 6 pilot accounts. Owner: Arjun Patel. Due: 2024-11-15.
2) Run pool-level sim sweep across 50 recent commits to quantify buffer size that achieves <2 low-util months per year. Owner: Maya Chen + SRE data. Due: 2024-10-18.
3) Prototype billing credit rule for off-peak recapture (sheet formulas + invoice preview) and run internal audit. Owner: Leah Gomez. Due: 2024-11-01.
4) Legal & Finance: draft contract language for dynamic overcommit insurance and run pricing sensitivity. Owner: Kai Morita. Due: 2024-12-01.

Risks / open questions:
- Customer perception risk: adding phase-in fees could be seen as nickel-and-diming; must be positioned as optional smoothing.
- Measurement: need consistent definition of "off-peak" across regions.
- Accounting: amortization policy changes will need coordination with Finance for revenue recognition and forecasting.

Quick checklist for making the sim reproducible:
- Copy sheet: adaptiveCurveSim -> adaptiveCurveSim_v2 (timestamped).
- Populate historical commit cadence for target test cohort (last 18 months).
- Ensure spot availability schedule plugged from infra SRE feed (tab: spot-availability).
- Run 1k Monte Carlo draws, export summary table of util percentiles.

- Simulation sheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1adaptiveCurveSim
